_anchor.title: The mid-market engagement
_anchor.terms: Outline & Co. delivers the strategy → identity → digital product flow for mid-market companies on fixed-price engagement scopes agreed at pitch. Standard engagement: 12-16 weeks. Standard deliverables: positioning document, identity system, digital product artefact (website, app, or design system).

components.label: Audience research
components._description: Interview the client's customers and stakeholders, transcribe and synthesise into an insights document feeding positioning.
components._body:
# Audience research

The strategy lead and one strategist run the audience-research interviews for an engagement. They transcribe and synthesise into an insights document that feeds [brand positioning](brand-positioning.md) (outline-roles-2025).

The four mid-level strategists run interviews and transcripts on assigned engagements; each strategist runs roughly four engagements per year, in parallel rather than serial (outline-roles-2025).

constraint_evidence.claim: The strategy lead and one strategist run interviews and synthesis; the skill is years of pattern-recognition not transferable.

components.label: Brand positioning
components._description: Author the positioning document for an engagement: how the client should be understood, against whom, with what proof points.
components._body:
# Brand positioning

The strategy lead writes the positioning document for every engagement. Inputs come from [audience research](audience-research.md) and the [competitive audit](competitive-audit.md); the output is a written brief that the [design lead](../people/lena-thorvaldsen.md) builds the identity system on top of (outline-roles-2025, outline-charter-2024 §1).

The artefact is owned by [Marco Bellini](../people/marco-bellini.md) and is not delegated — every positioning document goes out under his signature (outline-roles-2025).

constraint_evidence.claim: Authored personally by Marco on every engagement; not delegated. Charter §1.

components.label: Competitive audit
components._description: Map a client's competitive landscape: who else exists in the category, what they sound like, where the white space is.
components._body:
# Competitive audit

Strategists write competitive audits on briefed projects: who else exists in the category, what they sound like, where the white space is. The audit feeds the positioning brief (outline-roles-2025).

The strategy lead also does competitive-audit work for new pitches when the studio is in front of a prospect — the audit is the pitch's evidence base (outline-roles-2025).

constraint_evidence.claim: Strategists do this on briefed projects; the bottleneck is moving the audit findings into the positioning brief on time.

ai_evidence.claim: Closest tasks in the AEI sample show observed delegation in the upper-middle of the autonomy band; the activity is hand-off heavy and shared-knowledge would dissolve the trade-off.

components.label: Brand book
components._description: Author the brand book — the studio's signature artefact. Built personally by the design lead on every engagement.
components._body:
# Brand book

The design lead builds the brand book personally on every engagement. The brand book is the artefact the studio is best known for and the design lead does not delegate it (outline-roles-2025).

Mid-level designers may produce individual brand-book chapters under the lead's review, but the integration into a single artefact is the lead's hand (outline-roles-2025).

constraint_evidence.claim: Built personally by Lena on every engagement, not delegated.

components.label: Identity system build
components._description: Build the full identity system for an engagement: typography, colour, grid, motion, illustration direction, photo direction.
components._body:
# Identity system build

Senior designers run the identity-system build for individual engagements: typography, colour, grid, motion logic, illustration direction, photo direction. They typically own one engagement at a time (outline-roles-2025).

Mid-level designers support the senior on the system build. The design lead reviews every deliverable before it leaves the studio per the senior-eyes-on-every-output rule (outline-roles-2025, outline-charter-2024 §9).

constraint_evidence.claim: Senior designers run system builds, but every deliverable goes back to Lena for review — a hand-off bottleneck.

components.label: Visual language
components._description: Define the visual language for an engagement: typography, colour, imagery direction, motion logic, on top of the positioning brief.
components._body:
# Visual language

The design lead defines the visual language for the brief from strategy: typography choice, colour direction, imagery treatment, motion logic. The visual language feeds the [identity system build](identity-system-build.md) (outline-roles-2025).

constraint_evidence.claim: Defined by Lena on every engagement, not delegated. The studio's signature voice.

components.label: Design system build
components._description: Build a design system for clients who maintain their own product engineering. Documented system, ready for client handoff.
components._body:
# Design system build

Mid-level product designers own design-system documentation when the client is building a system the studio will hand off. The senior product designer leads the system architecture; the mid-level produces the documentation that lets the client team maintain it (outline-roles-2025).

The system build feeds the [asset handover](asset-handover.md) ritual at the end of the engagement.

constraint_evidence.claim: Mid-level product designers own documentation; the senior coordinates with the client team. The cost is hand-off, not the work itself.

ai_evidence.claim: Closest tasks in the AEI sample show observed delegation in the upper-middle of the autonomy band; the activity is hand-off heavy and shared-knowledge would dissolve the trade-off.

components.label: UI design
components._description: UI design for B2B web and apps: screens, components, interactions, accessibility, paired with client front-end engineers.
components._body:
# UI design

Senior product designers own UI design for individual engagements: screens, components, interactions, prototyping, accessibility audits, pairing with the client's front-end developers (outline-roles-2025).

The product lead reviews every UI deliverable; on enterprise engagements the lead or a senior typically embeds with the client product team for the duration (outline-roles-2025, outline-charter-2024 §16).

constraint_evidence.claim: Senior product designers run engagements; product lead reviews every deliverable — hand-off cost.

components.label: UX research
components._description: Embedded UX research with the client product team: usability testing, observation, synthesis.
components._body:
# UX research

The product lead runs UX research when the engagement asks for it: embedded with the client's product team, usability testing, observation, synthesis into a research report (outline-roles-2025).

User insights from research feed back into [UI design](ui-design.md) and into the [positioning](brand-positioning.md) brief on engagements where the strategy work hasn't yet closed.

constraint_evidence.claim: Product lead embeds with client product team; the cost is moving findings between embedded research and the design lead's brief.

components.label: Asset handover
components._description: Run the asset-handover ritual at the end of each engagement: delivery of all artefacts, sign-off, archival.
components._body:
# Asset handover

The client services lead manages the asset-handover ritual at the end of each engagement. The handover package collects the brand book, identity system files, design-system documentation, UI screens, and any source files the client owns under the contract (outline-roles-2025).

The relevant discipline lead is present at handover; the lead and Tomás together walk the client through what they're receiving and confirm sign-off (outline-roles-2025).

constraint_evidence.claim: Tomás runs handover with the discipline lead present. Coordinating who delivers what and when is the cost.

ai_evidence.claim: Closest tasks in the AEI sample show observed delegation in the upper-middle of the autonomy band; the activity is hand-off heavy and shared-knowledge would dissolve the trade-off.

components.label: Kickoff workshop
components._description: Run the kickoff workshop for every engagement: scope agreement, calendar, weekly cadence, single point of contact on client side.
components._body:
# Kickoff workshop

The client services lead runs the kickoff workshop for every engagement: scoping, calendar, weekly cadence agreement, single point of contact on the client side. The output is the engagement-scope document that anchors weekly check-ins, asset handovers, and the fixed-price agreement (outline-roles-2025, outline-charter-2024 §4, §12).

The relevant discipline lead sits at the kickoff alongside [Tomás Reis](../people/tomas-reis.md). Enterprise kickoffs additionally include the founder (outline-roles-2025).

constraint_evidence.claim: Tomás runs kickoff with the discipline lead. The cost is aligning on scope across four leads on day one.

ai_evidence.claim: Closest tasks in the AEI sample show observed delegation in the upper-middle of the autonomy band; the activity is hand-off heavy and shared-knowledge would dissolve the trade-off.

components.label: Weekly check-in
components._description: Run the weekly check-in call on each active engagement: progress, blockers, next-week scope confirmation.
components._body:
# Weekly check-in

Account managers run the weekly check-ins on three assigned engagements each. The lead [Tomás Reis](../people/tomas-reis.md) does not run weekly check-ins himself but reviews the notes and intervenes when an engagement is sliding (outline-roles-2025).

The weekly check-in is the rhythm of an Outline engagement; it's where scope drifts get caught, where client approvals get chased, and where the discipline lead is pulled in if the work needs adjustment (outline-roles-2025).

constraint_evidence.claim: Account managers run check-ins on three engagements each. The cost is keeping notes legible to Marco who reviews them.

mode_evidence.claim: In 2025 the studio ran 14 engagements; three needed founder-led scope renegotiation triggered by check-in notes that took weeks to surface a pattern.
Marco reviews every weekly check-in note across 14 active engagements per year; this is the studio's primary coordination mechanism between strategy, design, product, and client services.

bundle_state.coordination_paradox_risk: Shipping AI as an accelerator on UI design and design-system documentation — the production layer — without first deploying it as shared-knowledge infrastructure on kickoff, asset-handover and competitive-audit would speed the production teams while leaving the four discipline leads as the bottleneck. The asymmetry would make scope drift surface later, not sooner.

engine_candidates.evidence: Kickoff aligns four discipline leads + Tomás on scope, calendar, single point of contact. Today this happens in a 1-day workshop and the alignment degrades by week 4. Shared-knowledge infrastructure (prior engagement context auto-loaded; scope agreements queryable across the studio) would let any of the four leads stay aligned without all four being in the room.

Handover collects deliverables from four units and signs off with the client. Today Tomás coordinates manually across discipline leads. Shared-knowledge infrastructure would let the handover package self-assemble and let the discipline leads come in only for sign-off.

Today competitive audits are written for each engagement and live in delivered files. The same market knowledge gets re-derived on every engagement. Shared-knowledge infrastructure would let cumulative competitive context flow into each new pitch and audit.

rebundle_candidates.name: Compounding context: kickoff + handover wired into a single context loop
rebundle_candidates.description: Deploy a context-keeping practice that captures every engagement (positioning, visual language, brand book, market findings, scope changes) and feeds it into the next kickoff. Run by a new role — a context lead — who refreshes the picture at every engagement close.
rebundle_candidates.what_changes: Tomás runs kickoffs with prior context already loaded; the discipline leads stop being the bottleneck. Marco no longer reads every weekly note — only the ones the system flags. Returning clients get a kickoff that starts from where the last one ended.
rebundle_candidates.risk_of_rebundle: Conservative move. The new role is one hire; the system is internal-facing only. Risk is that the studio underbuilds the system (treats it as a wiki rather than a query layer). Mitigation: ship the use-case (returning-client kickoff) before the system.

rebundle_candidates.name: Production handed off, judgement kept in
rebundle_candidates.description: Spin out the production layer (UI design, design-system documentation, identity-system build) as a productized add-on that the studio offers at zero margin paired with strategy + identity engagements. The differentiated craft (positioning, visual language, brand book) becomes the studio's only billable product.
rebundle_candidates.what_changes: Pricing changes shape: the studio sells the differentiated work and bundles the production layer as included. Senior designer hours move upstream onto positioning briefs and brand-book authorship. The studio stops competing on UI quality (where AI levels the field) and competes on positioning + visual language only.
rebundle_candidates.risk_of_rebundle: Radical. Charter §15 names the strategy → identity → digital-product flow as the studio's positioning. Reframing the production layer as included rather than equally-priced is the kind of move that needs founder-led pricing conversations on every existing client. Risk: existing clients hear a price hike where the studio means a re-anchor.

decisions.question: What's actually expensive about delivering a mid-market engagement at this studio?
decisions.answer:
Eight of the twelve activities in scope are coordination-bound: the work itself isn't hard, the cost is moving information and decisions between four discipline leads (Marco, Lena, the product lead, Tomás) and across four units (strategy, design, digital-product, client-services). Today this coordination runs through Tomás's weekly check-in notes, which Marco reviews for every active engagement; in 2025 this surfaced three scope-renegotiation conversations weeks after the early signals appeared.

The other four activities are scarcity-bound — Marco's positioning craft, Lena's visual language and brand book, audience research synthesis. These are differentiated; the studio sells them by name. AI doesn't dissolve them.

decisions.question: Where would AI as shared-knowledge infrastructure actually change the structure of how the studio works?
decisions.answer:
Three places: kickoff workshops (where four leads align on scope), asset handover (where four units coordinate to close an engagement), and competitive audits (where market knowledge today gets re-derived from scratch on every engagement). Deployed as infrastructure on these three, AI changes a structural cost: the four leads stop being the bottleneck on alignment, and the studio's accumulated context starts compounding across engagements.

If instead the studio ships AI on UI design and design-system documentation — the production layer — it gets accelerator-effect only. The production teams move faster while the discipline leads are still the alignment bottleneck. The asymmetry makes scope drift surface later, not sooner.

decisions.question: Of the two direction options, which fits this studio next year?
decisions.answer:
The 'compounding context' option is the conservative move and the right first step: hire a context lead, ship the use-case (returning-client kickoff loaded with prior context), let the system grow from one use-case to the others. Risk is mostly internal; it doesn't change pricing or what the studio sells.

The 'production handed off, judgement kept in' option is the radical move and depends on the first one landing: only after the studio has compounded context across multiple engagements does it have the evidence base to reframe pricing around positioning + visual language and bundle the production layer as included. Doing it before would land as a price hike where the studio means a re-anchor.

Sequence: hire the context lead in Q3 2026; ship the returning-client kickoff use-case by Q4; revisit the pricing reframe in 2027 with twelve months of compounded context behind it.
